evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid office clerk in a monster-killing agency discovers his erased-outburst power can vaporize a regenerating British zombie — if he can stop panicking long enough to use it.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and has a clean genre promise: an underqualified desk worker gets dragged into a supernatural kill team. The comic ensemble, monster fight, and workplace absurdity give it a clear audience lane, though the very specific tonal flavor narrows the mass-market reach a bit.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages: Francis wakes in a surreal void, then gets pulled into Comirum’s death-toll bureaucracy and forced onto a field team. The wrist meter, the SINON reveal, and the London mission all establish the engine quickly and cleanly.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis has a strong comic-reluctant lead shape, and the team around him gives the movie multiple playable personalities. The characters are vivid in voice and behavior, with room for even more emotional contrast once the group dynamics deepen beyond the mission.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s blend of retro-futurist office satire, anomalous powers, and aggressively specific character comedy gives it a distinct identity. The comic-sans death board, the outburst meter, and the absurdly bureaucratic monster agency all feel like a confident point of view rather than generic genre dressing.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves briskly from office introduction to team assembly to London confrontation, and the central fight escalates cleanly. The middle is carried by banter and reveal rather than a deeply layered complication, but the momentum stays active and the climax pays off the setup.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a suppressed office worker whose power is tied to emotional eruption, inside a death-counting agency, feels fresh and immediately legible. It has that useful quality where the premise is strange on first glance but obvious in retrospect.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Comirum has a specific internal culture, visual language, and hierarchy, from the death-toll board to the retro-futuristic gear drops. The world feels story-generating, though this excerpt keeps the focus tight enough that the larger institutional ecosystem is only partially revealed.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is unmistakable: deadpan workplace comedy colliding with monster violence, profanity, and cartoonish character behavior. Francis, Clara, Toast, Hal, and Doreen all speak in a way that makes the script identifiable from dialogue alone.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are hints of deeper mythology in the SINON concept, Francis’s erased memory, and Doreen’s line about top brass wanting this. The script is currently playing the surface with confidence, and the emotional or mythic reserves are present more as suggestion than as a fully opened second layer.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The team has a lively combinatorial feel: Francis and Ploy, Clara and Hal, Clara and Toast, Doreen and everyone else all generate different comic energies. The ensemble is already functional as a machine for banter and mission friction, with enough distinct voices to keep scenes alive.

casting_characteristics: Ensemble of five principal teammates plus one boss and one antagonist
Francis requires a physically expressive comedic lead
Toast is a robot performance with voice and physicality
Clara is written with a strong specific accent/voice pattern
Ploy is bilingual and culturally specific in dialogue

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with one major exterior action sequence

technical.vfx_details: Multicolor energy effects, erasure/glow effects, a regenerating zombie, a robot character, and a few transformation-style weapon moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, limb loss, impact beats, weapon gags, and creature makeup/prosthetics for the British zombie.

rights_flags.detail: Microsoft Excel is referenced as a recognizable software equivalent.
Celtx appears in the script header as part of the document metadata.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or genre-forward theatrical indie
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform potential; the premise also supports franchise or sequel expansion if desired.

cost.note: Contained interiors and a single major action sequence keep the footprint manageable, while creature effects, energy VFX, and night exterior coverage push it above micro-budget.

cast.note: The ensemble is compact, but the project benefits from strong comic performers and a distinctive physical/voice cast for Francis, Toast, Clara, Ploy, and Doreen.

location.note: The story is largely contained to a few office interiors plus one London street sequence and nearby alley/rooftop coverage.

content.note: Monster violence, blood, profanity, drug references, and a decapitation-style creature fight place it in mature genre territory.

rights.note: The script uses a few recognizable brand references, but there is no heavy dependence on real people, music, or licensed IP.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The office is the monster world.
strengths.what_it_means: That inversion gives the movie a clean commercial identity: supernatural action built out of workplace routine, which makes the premise easy to market and easy to remember. Buyers who want genre with a comic engine — and actors who like playing bureaucracy as battle — will immediately understand the lane.
strengths.evidence: The death-toll board, cubicles, spreadsheet work, and Doreen’s briefing all happen before the team is sent into the field.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Francis is a strong reluctant-lead engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A lead who is visibly anxious, physically awkward, and secretly dangerous gives the movie a built-in audience surrogate and a performance centerpiece. That kind of role attracts actors looking for a comic breakout with action payoff, especially in the vein of a nervous outsider who becomes the key to the mission.
strengths.evidence: Francis starts the story asleep at his desk, panics through the briefing, insists he cannot do the job, and then detonates the zombie with a multicolor beam.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The team has immediate comic chemistry.
strengths.what_it_means: The ensemble gives the project repeatable scene energy and makes the movie feel castable as a group, not just a single lead vehicle. That is attractive to buyers because it supports trailer moments, quoteable banter, and a package built around several recognizable character types.
strengths.evidence: Hal’s swagger, Clara’s coke-fueled chaos, Toast’s deadpan logic, Ploy’s bass-heavy bravado, and Doreen’s hard-edged authority all collide in the briefing and on the street.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The SINON power is a sharp hook.
strengths.what_it_means: A power that appears to be tied to emotional release and unknown triggers gives the film a simple but flexible mythic engine. That creates room for sequels, spin-offs, or a franchise lane because the audience understands the rule without needing a dense exposition dump.
strengths.evidence: Francis’s wrist meter rises with his emotional state, and his final blast only arrives after he eats the hot dog and remembers the opening vision.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The British zombie is a memorable antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: The villain’s grotesque, comic, and culturally specific design gives the climax a strong visual signature and a clean trailer image. Creature-feature buyers and genre audiences respond to antagonists who can be described in one sentence and still feel like a full event.
strengths.evidence: The green-skinned, monocled, tea-sipping undead Brit regenerates after being shot apart and keeps fighting through the rooftop chase.

strengths.what_it_means: The comic-sans death board, 70s-style computer, brutalist weapon drops, and 1988 power-dress authority figure create a visual package that feels ownable in stills and marketing art. That kind of design language helps a producer sell the movie as a world, not just a plot.
strengths.evidence: The logistics office, the wrist device, and the gear that arrives in bright light all carry a consistent retro-futurist look.

whats_special.headline: This is a highly castable genre-comedy with a clean, marketable engine: a terrified office clerk in a monster bureaucracy discovers his emotional outbursts are the most dangerous weapon in the room. The script’s biggest asset is how confidently it turns workplace deadpan into supernatural action, giving producers a contained, trailer-friendly feature with a distinctive ensemble and a lead role actors can really seize.

lead_characters.name: Francis Booker
lead_characters.hook: Francis is a nervous, undercaffeinated office drone with a hidden cosmic fuse: he wants to stay invisible, keep his spreadsheet job, and avoid literally exploding, but the world keeps insisting he is the answer. He plays as a comic bundle of panic, self-protection, and buried power, with a face that can sell embarrassment, fear, and sudden awe in the same beat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network crossed with the physical-release arc of Simon Pegg in Shaun of the Dead — a fast-talking, tightly wound lead who gets to turn anxiety into heroism. Actors who can do brittle comedy, panic, and then land a genuine power-up moment will see this as a breakout role with franchise potential.

lead_characters.name: Ploy
lead_characters.hook: Ploy is all momentum, bass, and swagger, the kind of teammate who treats danger like a social event and speaks in a mix of flirtation, profanity, and fearless confidence. She reads as the friend who can clown you, save you, and call you out in the same breath, which makes her the movie’s most kinetic social force.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the showcase energy of Awkwafina in The Farewell or The Little Hours — a role that lets an actor weaponize timing, attitude, and vulnerability without ever losing the comic edge. Performers with strong voice, rhythm, and physical confidence will chase it because Ploy can steal scenes while still feeling like part of the team.

lead_characters.name: Hal
lead_characters.hook: Hal is the loud, swaggering bruiser who treats combat like a bar story and humiliation like a hobby. Beneath the macho noise, he has the easy confidence of someone who knows exactly how ridiculous he looks and enjoys it anyway.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Dave Bautista in Guardians of the Galaxy — a physically imposing character whose comedy comes from sincerity, timing, and the gap between size and self-image. Action-comedy performers and stunt-capable character actors will want the role because it gives them fight business, banter, and a memorable silhouette.

lead_characters.name: Clara
lead_characters.hook: Clara is a coke-fueled live wire with a knife in one hand, a cigarette in the other, and zero interest in behaving like a normal person. She’s flirtatious, volatile, funny, and dangerous, which makes her feel like she could kiss you, insult you, and shoot the room in the same minute.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Margot Robbie had in Birds of Prey — a feral, style-forward chaos engine that lets an actor play glamour, menace, and comic volatility at once. Actors who want a scene-stealing part with costume, attitude, and action will be drawn to her immediately.

lead_characters.name: Toast
lead_characters.hook: Toast is a dry, hyper-literal robot with a superiority complex and a body built for combat, but the comedy comes from how much personality leaks through the machine logic. He is the team’s deadpan scalpel: insulting, precise, and weirdly dependable when everything else is chaos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Alan Tudyk’s K-2SO in Rogue One — a voice-and-physical-performance role where the humor is in the timing, not the punchline. Performers with strong vocal control and motion-capture or suit performance chops will want it because the character can become a fan favorite fast.

lead_characters.name: Doreen
lead_characters.hook: Doreen is the hard-edged boss who runs the room with clipped authority, a power-dress silhouette, and the kind of calm that makes everyone else look unserious. She is all institutional pressure and dry contempt, but the brief flashes of empathy suggest she knows exactly how broken the machine is.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of command role Frances McDormand had in Fargo — a contained authority figure whose stillness makes every line land harder. Character actors who can project intelligence, control, and a hint of private fatigue will chase it because Doreen can anchor the whole agency in a few scenes.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make monster action feel like office comedy with teeth.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Second- or third-feature directors, or TV genre directors moving into features, who already have a handle on ensemble timing and stylized world-building. This material rewards filmmakers who like performance-forward action, crisp visual design, and tonal control over heavy spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a contained playground where character banter, creature design, and action choreography all need to feel like one language. It will appeal to directors who want to prove they can stage a clean, funny, effects-assisted feature without losing the human rhythm of the scenes.

buyer_appeal.detail: The contained cast and limited location footprint make this viable without a star-heavy package, though a recognizable comic lead would help open the movie. The monster-comedy lane travels well on streamers and at genre festivals because the premise is instantly legible and the creature payoff is trailer-friendly.

considerations.area: Francis’s trigger can be foregrounded earlier.
considerations.detail: The opening vision, the wrist meter, and the final hot-dog payoff all point to a clear emotional-mechanics engine. A next pass could seed one more early moment where Francis’s body reacts before he understands why, so the climax feels even more inevitable and the audience tracks the rule sooner.

considerations.area: The team chemistry could carry one more turn.
considerations.detail: The briefing-room assembly and London banter already establish a fun ensemble rhythm. One direction would be to give one pair inside the team a sharper private dynamic before the fight, so the group feels even more like a unit with history rather than only a mission-ready lineup.

considerations.area: The climax is built on a single location run.
considerations.detail: The London street, alley, and rooftop sequence is the only major exterior action stretch, which keeps the movie producible but concentrates the finale’s geography. If needed, the version of the set-piece where the alley and rooftop beats are collapsed more tightly would protect momentum and simplify coverage without changing the payoff.

considerations.area: The brand references are light but present.
considerations.detail: The script names Microsoft Excel and uses a Celtx header in the sample pages, which are easy to clear or replace. A cleaner pass could swap those references for generic equivalents if the goal is to keep the legal footprint as light as possible.
